claimText: Commonly encountered in and around forest reserves and some parkland. Feeding changes natural foraging behaviour and increases conflict.
note: AVS describes daytime foraging, forest-edge encounters, feeding effects and the stated encounter precautions.

claimText: Keep food out of sight, secure bags and give the group space. Do not stare, feed, tease or try to touch a monkey.
note: AVS describes daytime foraging, forest-edge encounters, feeding effects and the stated encounter precautions.

claimText: Roots through the ground for food. Females may travel with young; an animal with piglets or no escape route needs particular space.
note: AVS covers soil digging, protective mothers, road conflict, feeding effects and distance from piglets.

claimText: An omnivore whose rooting changes soil and leaf litter.
note: AVS covers soil digging, protective mothers, road conflict, feeding effects and distance from piglets.

claimText: Human food, roads and encounters near urban edges can lead to conflict. Never encourage it to approach people.
note: AVS covers soil digging, protective mothers, road conflict, feeding effects and distance from piglets.

claimText: Stay calm, keep your distance and avoid separating adults from piglets. Do not feed or corner a boar.
note: AVS covers soil digging, protective mothers, road conflict, feeding effects and distance from piglets.

claimText: Widespread and commonly seen near people. Its national assessment is Not Applicable because it is introduced.
note: AVS confirms introduced, abundant urban occurrence; the NParks national table assigns Not Applicable.

claimText: Common in secondary woodland, gardens, parks and other urban greenery. It is a native resident, not an introduced noise-making species.
note: AVS records secondary forest, parks and urban habitat; the national table confirms native origin.

claimText: Loss of fruiting trees removes food. Managing noise complaints should not involve disturbing wildlife nests.
note: Fruit dependence supports the food-tree inference. NParks nesting guidance supports avoiding nest disturbance during noise complaints.

claimText: Least Concern · 2016
note: The research paper explicitly cites BirdLife International (2016) for this taxon's Least Concern status.

claimText: Widespread in parks, gardens and other wooded settings. It is listed as native and nationally Least Concern.
note: The ecology account confirms parks, gardens and wooded sites; the national table confirms native origin and Least Concern.

claimText: Blue-green upperparts with a white collar and belly. The large bill is dark, unlike the red bill of a white-throated kingfisher.
note: The species account confirms blue upperparts, white collar and black bill; the comparative article covers the white-throated species.

claimText: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
note: ADW supports one precocial young and roughly five months' gestation; the Ubin study independently records a juvenile.

claimText: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
note: The 2016 paper documents offshore rediscovery in 2005 and later mainland records. RDB3 confirms native, nationally Critically Endangered.

claimText: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
note: Chua et al. (2013) documents the additional localities, alongside earlier central-reserve records. Survey detections are not population estimates.

claimText: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
note: Chua et al. (2013) documents the additional localities, alongside earlier central-reserve records. Survey detections are not population estimates.

claimText: A documented Singapore nesting observation found a chick in a bird's-nest fern in 2016. Such records establish local breeding, but do not provide a complete island-wide breeding calendar.
note: The April 2016 direct observation documents a chick in a bird's-nest fern, not an island-wide breeding season.

claimText: Bird Society of Singapore lists it as an uncommon resident that favours dense woodland and mangroves. NParks has also documented use of the Eco-Link@BKE wildlife bridge; the bridge is not a public viewing site.
note: The bird account supports resident habitat. NParks confirms bridge use and research-only access.

claimText: A common native frog of suburban and rural greenery, as well as disturbed forest. It is nationally Least Concern in RDB3.
note: The ecology account supports human habitation and forest-edge occurrence; RDB3 confirms native origin and Least Concern.

claimText: Grey and white plumage, long legs, a long neck and a yellowish pointed bill. Adults have a dark stripe extending behind the eye.
note: ADW's physical, feeding and behaviour sections support this field. Food-web transfer is a qualitative inference.

claimText: Fish and other small animals captured near water.
note: ADW's physical, feeding and behaviour sections support this field. Food-web transfer is a qualitative inference.

claimText: Can feed during daylight or at night, depending on conditions.
note: ADW's physical, feeding and behaviour sections support this field. Food-web transfer is a qualitative inference.

claimText: Often waits motionless before striking at prey. It usually draws its neck back during flight.
note: ADW's physical, feeding and behaviour sections support this field. Food-web transfer is a qualitative inference.

claimText: Transfers energy from aquatic prey into the wider wetland food web.
note: ADW's physical, feeding and behaviour sections support this field. Food-web transfer is a qualitative inference.

claimText: Mainly active during daylight in the canopy.
note: The behaviour account supports daytime canopy activity and social families. NParks confirms the specialised digestive stomach.

claimText: Lives in social groups and spends much of its time in trees. Its specialised stomach supports digestion of leafy food.
note: The behaviour account supports daytime canopy activity and social families. NParks confirms the specialised digestive stomach.

claimText: Small population size and fragmented forest make protection of habitat and connectivity important.
note: NParks describes a small restricted population and canopy connections, including rope bridges. Habitat protection is the stated conservation response.

claimText: Broad snout, armoured body and a muscular, flattened tail. Only the eyes and nostrils may show above the surface.
note: NParks confirms broad snout and compressed muscular tail; ADW confirms eyes and nostrils can remain exposed above water.

claimText: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
note: ADW describes gliding and apparently solitary behaviour with limited study. The Singapore paper documents a tree-cavity nest.

claimText: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
note: Physical description confirms dark extremities, pale forehead strip, dorsal lines and variable markings.

claimText: A bulky grey-brown body, blunt bristled muzzle, paired front flippers and a fluked tail. It has no dorsal fin.
note: ADW describes brown-grey skin, bristled rounded muzzle, paired foreflippers, fluked tail and absence of a dorsal fin.

claimText: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
note: The zoo's species account confirms live birth. The local field paper does not establish the withheld Singapore breeding timetable.

claimText: An egg-laying snake. Do not disturb hidden snakes, egg sites or shelter; young snakes must also be left alone.
note: The taxon record explicitly lists egg-laying reproduction. Leaving snakes and eggs alone is conservative wildlife guidance.

claimText: Lays eggs; local nesting timing and clutch sizes have not been verified.
note: The taxon record explicitly lists egg-laying reproduction. No unverified local breeding measurements are added.

claimText: Lays eggs. Local nesting dates, clutch size and incubation periods are not asserted from unrelated captive accounts.
note: The species record confirms egg-laying reproduction without relying on captive accounts of related monitors.

claimText: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
note: The rediscovery paper confirms the 2008 Ubin record. The 2025 NParks update names greater mousedeer in continuing habitat work.

claimText: NParks documents catchment-forest records from 2006 and 2007. These are historical observations, while RDB3 (2024) retains the species as nationally Critically Endangered; neither is a current population census.
note: NParks lists the 2006 and 2007 catchment records. RDB3 supplies the separate current national category, not a census.

claimText: Native populations are associated with the Central Nature Reserves. The national assessment is Endangered in RDB3; encounter locations and resting sites are not mapped here.
note: NParks confines native populations to the central reserves. RDB3 lists Endangered, replacing the older profile's national category.

claimText: A familiar migrant at Sungei Buloh and other wetlands, including pond and canal edges. NParks records it throughout the year, with higher numbers commonly between November and January.
note: The two NParks accounts confirm wetland occurrence, year-round records and the November–January peak. They do not promise sightings.

claimText: Builds nests and lays eggs, often in colonies with other waterbirds. Both parents contribute to care. These species-level notes do not claim a local breeding colony.
note: The breeding account documents colonial nests, eggs and care by both parents. It does not establish a Singapore colony.

claimText: Fish are important prey, alongside frogs, aquatic invertebrates and other small animals; diet varies with habitat and prey availability.
note: The feeding, breeding and conservation sections support the field. Regional findings are not presented as Singapore measurements.

claimText: Builds a platform of reeds or sticks in wetland vegetation; trees and thickets can also be used. Both parents incubate and feed the young. Regional breeding seasons and clutch sizes vary, so none is presented here as a Singapore norm.
note: The feeding, breeding and conservation sections support the field. Regional findings are not presented as Singapore measurements.

claimText: The Heron Specialist Group identifies wetland alteration and disturbance as pressures across its range. Retaining suitable vegetated feeding and nesting habitat is a relevant local priority; no current Singapore decline rate is asserted.
note: The feeding, breeding and conservation sections support the field. Regional findings are not presented as Singapore measurements.

claimText: NParks records it in forest reserves and Pulau Ubin and highlights it in woodland birdwatching at Kranji Marshes. Bird Society lists it as a common resident; frequency of observation does not remove its national Vulnerable status.
note: NParks records the named sites; Bird Society supplies resident frequency. The RDB3 Vulnerable category remains separate.

claimText: Common in gardens, parks and other built environments. Being well established is different from being native.
note: NParks confirms common urban occurrence; the Singapore introduction study distinguishes established occurrence from native origin.

claimText: Least Concern · 2022
note: The author-uploaded IUCN report lists Least Concern and publication year 2022. Its assessment date is 29 December 2021. This is not a new 2026 assessment.

claimText: Least Concern · 2021
note: The IUCN report lists Least Concern, published in 2021, assessed on 8 May 2018. Publication year and assessment date differ.

claimText: Least Concern · 2018
note: The IUCN report lists Least Concern, published in 2018, assessed on 2 September 2011. It includes the Malayopython synonym.

claimText: Often nocturnal or hidden during daylight.
note: NParks describes generally nocturnal activity and daytime concealment in urban drains. This does not imply exclusively night activity.

claimText: Fish and other animals taken around waterways; also scavenges.
note: The feeding account supports aquatic prey and scavenging. The conservation section identifies disturbance and loss of breeding trees. Food-web position is qualitative.

claimText: A high-level predator and scavenger associated with aquatic food webs.
note: The feeding account supports aquatic prey and scavenging. The conservation section identifies disturbance and loss of breeding trees. Food-web position is qualitative.

claimText: Protecting large nesting trees and limiting disturbance helps keep suitable habitat available.
note: The feeding account supports aquatic prey and scavenging. The conservation section identifies disturbance and loss of breeding trees. Food-web position is qualitative.

claimText: Diurnal, often soaring above water.
note: ADW explicitly lists diurnal activity. The Peregrine Fund describes soaring over coastal and inland water bodies.

claimText: Follow park warnings and stay on designated paths. Keep well away from water edges, do not feed, and alert park staff to unsafe encounters.
note: AVS directs visitors to marked paths, away from water edges, and prohibits feeding. Its encounter advice includes reporting concerns to NParks.

claimText: Do not block a turtle’s route or use bright lights around nests. Observe from a distance and report nesting to NParks.
note: NParks turtle guidance supports distance, no lights, no interference and reporting nests. Keeping the route clear is conservative non-interference advice.

claimText: Associated with tall forest in the Central Nature Reserves and connected wooded spaces. A quiet, hidden animal may be present even when visitors do not notice it.
note: Flora & Fauna Web names the central reserves and adjacent parkland. BiodiversitySG explains tall-forest use, camouflage and concealed daytime rest.

claimText: Do not handle a bat or disturb a roost. Observe from a distance and seek professional help for an injured animal.
note: AVS gives non-handling and professional rescue advice. The roost and fruit dependence supports the qualitative habitat-loss inference, not a measured decline.

claimText: Loss of roosts and fruiting vegetation can remove shelter and food.
note: AVS gives non-handling and professional rescue advice. The roost and fruit dependence supports the qualitative habitat-loss inference, not a measured decline.

claimText: An omnivore. Regional research records fruit and other plant material, some animal food and mushrooms; the proportions in Singapore have not been measured here.
note: The 2026 paper documents mushroom feeding in Indonesia in 2020 and reviews other foods. It explicitly states that spore dispersal remains unproven.

claimText: Consumes material from several parts of the forest food web. Mushroom eating is documented, but effective fungal-spore dispersal by this species remains a research question.
note: The 2026 paper documents mushroom feeding in Indonesia in 2020 and reviews other foods. It explicitly states that spore dispersal remains unproven.

claimText: Lays eggs. Breeding has been achieved in conservation collections; no Singapore nesting month or clutch-size claim is made here.
note: The zoo account and Durrell breeding report document eggs and captive breeding. Captive timing is not a Singapore nesting calendar.

claimText: Common in buildings and nearby wooded areas. It is listed in Singapore’s national reptile assessment as Least Concern.
note: The Jurong Lake Gardens gecko section confirms buildings and nearby forests. RDB3 separately supplies the national Least Concern category.

claimText: A native resident of wooded areas and some neighbourhoods. The name Sumatran palm civet follows NParks’ current species table.
note: BiodiversitySG uses Paradoxurus musangus and describes forests and gardens. AVS adds neighbourhood occurrence under the older name; RDB3 confirms native status.

claimText: Associated with patches of mature forest in the Central Nature Reserves. It is nationally Critically Endangered in RDB3; this guide avoids breeding-site directions.
note: The Singapore field paper confines occurrence to the central reserves. RDB3 replaces its historical national category with Critically Endangered.

claimText: A bushy tail and a pale stripe above a darker stripe on each flank are useful clues. Check side markings, rather than relying on coat colour alone.
note: The Handbook taxonomic treatment explicitly places the pale flank stripe above the black stripe and describes regional colour variation. NParks supplies the bushy tail.

claimText: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
note: NParks confirms both underside colours, rusty membrane edges, round head and flattened feather-like tail. The field account adds the large eyes.

claimText: Lives among fallen leaves. Its rapid rattling call can be easier to notice than its camouflaged body.
note: NParks supports leaf-litter habitat. The dated Singapore field recording documents the rapid rattling call; detectability is viewing advice, not a measured probability.

claimText: Do not catch it by the tail. Avoid glue traps and let it move away normally.
note: NParks documents defensive tail loss; ACRES records gecko rescue from glue traps. Non-handling and trap avoidance follow those risks.

claimText: An adaptable omnivore eating insects, fruit and other available food.
note: The observer documents fruit, insects and human food use with linked photographs. This supports the omnivore summary, not measured diet proportions.

claimText: An urban omnivore that also competes for food and nesting cavities.
note: NParks identifies competition for food and nesting resources; the direct observations confirm varied feeding and cavity use.

claimText: A scavenger and omnivore, with possible effects on other birds’ eggs and young.
note: The NUS record documents predation and reviews local egg and nestling records, alongside carrion and refuse feeding. No population effect is quantified.

claimText: Builds a cup-like nest suspended in a fork of branches. Eggs and young stay protected within the nest.
note: The bird society describes the suspended cup nest and large-tree use. Retaining nesting trees and food plants is a habitat recommendation, not a Singapore decline estimate.

claimText: Retention of mature trees and food plants supports nesting and foraging.
note: The bird society describes the suspended cup nest and large-tree use. Retaining nesting trees and food plants is a habitat recommendation, not a Singapore decline estimate.

claimText: Least Concern · 2024
note: Cornell explicitly gives Least Concern and cites BirdLife's 2024 IUCN record, e.T22679199A263732457. The year is the cited publication year.

claimText: Forages within dense foliage; often heard before it is seen.
note: NParks Habitat and ecology describes feeding in dense foliage and frequent vocal detection. Replaced the unsupported daily-cycle label with these documented activities.

claimText: Moves through wooded areas and the tree canopy, giving loud cackling calls.
note: NParks describes movement through wooded areas, canopy use and loud cackling calls. Removed the unsourced daily-cycle classification.

claimText: Travels between feeding grounds and nesting beaches. These journeys can cross large areas of sea.
note: NOAA describes travel between foraging grounds and nesting beaches. The replacement does not claim a Singapore route, distance or schedule.

claimText: Access to human food can change behaviour and increase conflict with people. Keep food and rubbish secure.
note: AVS links access to human food with changed behaviour and conflict. Removed habitat fragmentation from this claim because the cited advisory does not measure that effect.

claimText: Care advice: do not feed squirrels. Let them forage for their natural food.
note: NParks advises against feeding wildlife. The profile source describes natural foraging. This is care advice, not a measured local population trend.

claimText: Attempts to catch or handle civets can cause stress or injury. Use NParks guidance for encounters around homes.
note: AVS warns that handling can stress or injure civets and gives advice for roof and property encounters. Removed unsupported claims about local shelter loss and road mortality.

claimText: Females give birth to live young and keep their fawns hidden. Breeding schedules vary across its range.
note: The Handbook of the Mammals of the World account describes pregnancy, births and hidden fawns. Regional breeding dates are not presented as a Singapore season.

claimText: Loss of lowland forest can reduce its habitat. Its response to forest disturbance varies across its range.
note: The account identifies lowland forest loss but reports variable responses to disturbance. Corrected the earlier blanket claim about mature-forest dependence.

claimText: Forages on the ground and in trees, often near people.
note: NParks explicitly describes ground and tree foraging near people. Removed the daily-cycle and evening-roost statements from this field.

claimText: Small animals, fruit, grain, eggs, carrion and accessible food waste.
note: The NUS record lists small vertebrates, grain, fruit, eggs, carrion and human refuse. This supports the revised food list.

claimText: Daytime activity is documented in Singapore. This does not establish an exclusively daytime activity cycle.
note: The observation occurred at about 14:55 on 15 June 2023. It supports daytime activity, not an exclusively daytime cycle.

claimText: Common in urban areas and also found in mangroves. NParks lists it as introduced; its national category is Not Applicable.
note: NParks lists urban and mangrove habitats and introduced origin. RDB3 records Not Applicable. Removed the redundant broader coastal-habitat wording.

claimText: Forages in fruiting trees, sometimes joining mixed flocks.
note: NParks Habitat and ecology explicitly describes mixed flocks at fruiting trees. Replaced the unsupported daily-cycle label with observed foraging behaviour.

claimText: Watches for prey from a fence, wire or low branch, then flies down to catch it.
note: NParks describes hunting from fences, wires and low branches. This source does not quantify a full daily activity cycle.

claimText: Nests in cavities. A Singapore study recorded a pair nesting in a canal-bank opening. Keep away from occupied nests.
note: The NUS canal study documents an occupied nesting cavity and adults bringing food. Ethical guidance supports keeping away from occupied nests.

claimText: Suitable nesting sites need protection. NParks has installed nest boxes for kingfishers and woodpeckers on Coney Island.
note: NParks chapter 11, page 167, records nest boxes for kingfishers and woodpeckers on Coney Island. Reframed the unmeasured pressure as habitat-care advice.

claimText: Native wild birds and admixed free-ranging birds occur locally. The national Near Threatened assessment applies to the wild species, not all domestic chickens.
note: NParks describes mixed domestic-fowl and red-junglefowl flocks on the mainland. RDB3 assigns Near Threatened to Gallus gallus, not every free-ranging domestic chicken. The article's older Endangered label is not used; the dated RDB3 table controls the national category.

claimText: Females lay eggs in ground nests and care for their chicks.
note: The Singapore field guide describes a ground nest and eggs. ADW describes chicks remaining with their mother. Removed the unsupported precise timing of independent feeding.

claimText: Pursues prey and can climb trees. When threatened, it may escape from a branch into water.
note: ADW describes pursuit hunting, climbing trees and dropping into water to escape predators. Replaced the unsupported basking and chemical-sampling wording.

claimText: Females lay eggs beside decaying logs or stumps.
note: ADW Reproduction states that females deposit eggs along rotting logs or stumps. Removed unsupported claims about soil sites and immediate independence.

claimText: NParks reports poaching of monitor lizards in Singapore. Do not buy live monitors, their meat or skin products.
note: AVS Conservation explicitly reports monitor-lizard poaching in Singapore and advises against buying animals, meat and skin products. No mortality rate is inferred.

claimText: Ambushes prey and kills by constriction. It can climb trees as well as move on the ground.
note: ADW describes ambush, constriction, ground movement and tree climbing. No claim about exclusive terrestrial activity remains.

claimText: Lays eggs; the female coils around the clutch during incubation. Eggs and resting snakes must not be moved by visitors.
note: ADW explicitly describes egg laying and female coiling during incubation. AVS says to leave snakes alone and avoid handling. The final sentence is visitor advice.

claimText: Handling or cornering a python can cause stress or injury and provoke a defensive bite.
note: AVS warns that handling can cause stress or injury and a defensive bite. Replaced unquantified road-collision and persecution statements with the supported encounter risk.

claimText: Attempts to catch or handle snakes can cause stress or injury. Leave rescue work to trained professionals.
note: AVS advises against handling snakes because it can cause stress or injury, and directs rescue work to trained staff. No local killing rate is claimed.

claimText: Back away and keep people and pets away. Never try to catch it. Seek urgent medical care after a bite or venom entering the eyes.
note: AVS supports slow retreat, keeping pets away, no handling and immediate medical attention after a bite. The clinical case report supports urgent treatment of venom in the eyes. No drug or home-treatment advice is added.

claimText: Glue traps can catch geckos as well as their intended targets.
note: ACRES photograph confirms a trapped gecko. Removed pesticide claim.

claimText: Shelters under rocks and in drains. When threatened, it can inflate its body.
note: NParks records shelter under rocks and in drains, plus inflation when threatened. Removed the unsupported climbing and call-distance comparison.

claimText: Breeding groups gather near ponds, puddles and ditches to lay eggs.
note: NParks Habitat and ecology describes breeding gatherings and egg laying beside ponds, puddles and ditches. The replacement stays within that evidence.

claimText: Eats small insects and is prey for monitor lizards.
note: NParks describes consumption of ants, termites and other insects. The AVS monitor page identifies a banded bullfrog in a clouded monitor's mouth.

claimText: Care advice: do not release frogs or tadpoles into new sites. Introduced animals can disrupt local ecosystems.
note: NParks explains harm from introduced animals and advises against releases. This is prevention advice; it does not allege a measured local traffic effect.

claimText: Not assessed here
note: The complete published RDB3 amphibian table has no Kaloula pulchra row. Not assessed here is this guide's explicit limitation, not an official NE, NA or threat category.

claimText: Care advice: protect plants around breeding water. Do not disturb foam nests above ponds and drains.
note: NParks documents foam nests on vegetation or walls over water. The replacement gives habitat-care advice based on that breeding requirement. It does not claim a quantified pollution effect.

claimText: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
note: ADW describes live young, maternal provisioning and weaning. NUS reports an apparent juvenile and states that the relationship of observed pairs was uncertain. These sources support the existing qualified wording.

claimText: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
note: ADW identifies deforestation, habitat degradation and occasional meat or pet trade in parts of Southeast Asia. The profile correctly avoids claiming a measured Singapore exploitation rate.

claimText: Perches beside water, then dives to catch fish and invertebrates.
note: The Bird Society account describes perching, head and tail movements and diving for prey. Replaced the unsupported daytime qualifier.

claimText: Usually feeds alone, stalking prey along mudflat and estuary edges.
note: The Bird Society account describes solitary stalking at mudflat and estuary edges. Removed the unsupported daytime qualifier.

claimText: Diurnal; hunts, perches and soars during the day.
note: The Peregrine Fund explicitly identifies this as a diurnal raptor and describes exposed perching, soaring and hunting. This supports the whole activity field.

claimText: A resident species recorded in freshwater wetlands and coastal vegetation. NParks lists the Central Catchment, Sungei Buloh and Pulau Ubin. It can be familiar at suitable wetlands while remaining nationally Endangered.
note: NParks Flora and Fauna Web names Central Catchment, Sungei Buloh and Pulau Ubin. The Bird Society confirms resident wetland occurrence. RDB3, not the older profile, supplies national Endangered.

claimText: A broad, angular head with pointed eyelid projections and a leaf-like snout. Its brown body resembles dead leaves. Females are larger than males.
note: ADW supports leaf-like colour, angular head and eyelid/nasal projections. The NUS field paper confirms larger females. Removed unsupported variation in projection length.

claimText: Waits motionless in leaf litter and ambushes passing prey. Singapore researchers have recorded males calling beside forest streams.
note: ADW describes motionless ambush in leaf litter. NUS documents frequent male calls along a stream and distinctive calls. Removed the disputed loudness description.

claimText: Lives among forest leaf litter in the Central Nature Reserves. RDB3 lists it as nationally Near Threatened.
note: NParks Flora and Fauna Web places it in the Central Nature Reserves and leaf litter. RDB3 supplies Near Threatened. Removed the separate survey-frequency claim.

claimText: Watch without touching, feeding or blocking its path. Report a stranded animal to the NParks Animal Response Centre.
note: Queensland's general marine-mammal guidance supports no touching, feeding or blocking travel. These are care principles, not imported Singapore legal distances. NParks supplies the local wildlife contact.

claimText: NParks includes Sousa chinensis in Singapore's marine mammal list and records it as nationally Critically Endangered. The list does not provide a population count or guarantee sightings.
note: The NParks marine-mammal RDB3 list names Sousa chinensis and national Critically Endangered. Removed the separate island-sighting claim rather than imply that a status table proves sightings.

claimText: Do not chase, feed or block a dolphin's path. Report a stranded animal to the NParks Animal Response Centre.
note: OPCFHK identifies chasing and course interception as harmful. Queensland guidance supports no feeding or path blocking; no foreign legal distances are applied. NParks supplies the local wildlife contact.

claimText: Loss of nesting trees, disturbance near colonies and water pollution can harm herons. These are range-wide pressures, not measured Singapore trends.
note: The Heron Specialist Group describes harm from nesting-tree removal, nearby operations and water pollution. The replacement explicitly treats these as range-wide evidence, not measured Singapore trends.

claimText: Not separately assessed · broader taxon 2024
note: Compared the exact scientific name, IUCN taxonomy and Global threat-status extension in the IUCN-published GBIF dataset, retrieved 7 September 2026. claimText: Most Singapore records are of juveniles, which are most likely to be confused with Japanese Sparrowhawk and Shikra. Compared to juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, juvenile Besra has thicker dark undertail bands (visible when tail is spread), longer tail, more rounded wings, smaller head relative to body, and usually fewer primary bars. The yellow orbital ring and broader dark undertail bands separate it from juvenile Shikra. Adult plumages recall the Crested Goshawk, which is larger, shows six fingers in flight, and has more rounded wings. Male has cinnamon-rufous breast with a prominent dark mesial stripe; female is similar but is usually browner above.

claimText: Male has dark grey upperparts, pinkish-rufous barring on underparts, reddish eyes with yellow eyering, and yellow cere; mesial stripe faint or absent. Female about 15% larger, with browner upperparts, yellowish eyes, and grey-barred underparts. Juvenile has darker brown upperparts, white supercilium, streaked or spotted breast, and broken bars on flanks. In flight, shows five fingers and is broader-winged than Chinese Sparrowhawk (which has four fingers). claimText: Juvenile birds are similar to Japanese Sparrowhawk and Besra. From juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, key differences include the proportionally longer tail, more rounded wings, often thicker and longer mesial stripe, and grey (not yellow) eyering. Juvenile Besra has broader dark undertail bands and a yellow (not grey) orbital ring. Adult male has red iris, orange-barred underparts, and plain grey upperparts with black wingtips; central tail feathers unbarred. Adult female similar but has yellow iris and browner upperparts. Differs from Chinese Sparrowhawk by having five fingers (vs. four) and broader, more rounded wings.

claimText: In all plumages, differs from other sparrowhawks by narrow pointed wings showing only four fingers in flight and nearly unmarked underwing-coverts. Adult male has uniform grey upperparts, red irides, dark grey orbital ring, orange-yellow cere, pinkish-orange breast, and obvious black wingtips. Female similar but with browner upperparts, yellow irides, and less uniform orange underparts. Juvenile has rufous-barred flanks and occasionally a mesial stripe, making them superficially similar to juvenile Grey-faced Buzzard, but that species has much longer and less pointed wings. Besra, Shikra, and Japanese Sparrowhawk have five fingers; Crested Goshawk and Eurasian Sparrowhawk have six.

claimText: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.

claimText: The Buteo buzzards present a stocky body and broad wings when in flight. Difficult to distinguish from Eastern Buzzard, but said to be darker brown overall, with dark carpal patch not contrasting with the rest of the wing as strongly. Can come in three distinct morphs: brown, rufous and dark. Brown morph with solid, brown wing lining and often possessing a pale breast 'belt' that separates the dark plumage of the belly from the strong upper breast streaking; tail also strongly barred. Rufous morph has dark brown underparts of brown morph replaced by warm rufous brown and less distinct tail barring. Dark morph has blackish-brown body plumage with pale flight feathers and a dark trailing edge to the wing. Crested Honey Buzzard shows a small protruding head and longer tail; Changeable Hawk-Eagle is larger with a prominent crest; Jerdon's Baza has a long crest and strongly barred underparts.

claimText: Good views are needed to separate this species from Common Kestrel. Male has grey head, plain rufous-chestnut mantle and median coverts, grey upperwing coverts and tertials, and buffish underparts with fewer, rounder spots than Common Kestrel. Female is brownish with barred upperparts, indistinct moustachial/cheek stripe and no dark line behind eye; juvenile almost identical to female. Differences from Common Kestrel: pale yellow claws (Common Kestrel has black claws), proportionately longer central tail feathers, and proportionately shorter outermost primary – p10 shorter than p8 (in Common Kestrel, p10 is as long as p8).

claimText: Smaller, narrower-winged, and slimmer overall than Peregrine Falcon. Male is distinctive with pale grey upperparts, strikingly white underwing-coverts, rufous-chestnut vent, and diagnostic red eyering, cere and feet. Female and juvenile best distinguished from Eurasian Hobby by the pale, two-toned underwing with pronounced dark trailing edge. Female has dark streaked underparts, barred uppertail-coverts, buffy-white vent and grey upperparts. Juvenile has pale yellow eyering and cere, and shows a distinct pale neck-band and barred underwing, separating it from juvenile Eurasian Hobby, which lacks the pale collar (thus appearing darker-faced) and has a uniformly dark underwing.

claimText: Adult has slate-blue upperparts, heavily streaked underparts on a whitish background, reddish-rufous thighs and vent, and a dark moustachial stripe set off by white cheeks and throat. claimText: The migratory subspecies calidus has slaty-grey upperparts, white or buffish underparts with dark bars, broad blackish moustachial streak and white ear coverts. claimText: Most Singapore records are of juveniles, which are most likely to be confused with Japanese Sparrowhawk and Shikra. Compared to juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, juvenile Besra has thicker dark undertail bands (visible when tail is spread), longer tail, more rounded wings, smaller head relative to body, and usually fewer primary bars. The yellow orbital ring and broader dark undertail bands separate it from juvenile Shikra. Adult plumages recall the Crested Goshawk, which is larger, shows six fingers in flight, and has more rounded wings. Male has cinnamon-rufous breast with a prominent dark mesial stripe; female is similar but is usually browner above.

claimText: Male has dark grey upperparts, pinkish-rufous barring on underparts, reddish eyes with yellow eyering, and yellow cere; mesial stripe faint or absent. Female about 15% larger, with browner upperparts, yellowish eyes, and grey-barred underparts. Juvenile has darker brown upperparts, white supercilium, streaked or spotted breast, and broken bars on flanks. In flight, shows five fingers and is broader-winged than Chinese Sparrowhawk (which has four fingers). Juveniles may be confused with juvenile Besra and juvenile Shikra, but those species have proportionally smaller heads, more rounded wings, and proportionally longer tail. Eurasian Sparrowhawk is larger, lacks mesial stripe, has six fingers, and a longer tail. Crested Goshawk differs by having six fingers, very prominent mesial stripe, and much more rounded wings.

claimText: In all plumages, differs from other sparrowhawks by narrow pointed wings showing only four fingers in flight and nearly unmarked underwing-coverts. Adult male has uniform grey upperparts, red irides, dark grey orbital ring, orange-yellow cere, pinkish-orange breast, and obvious black wingtips. Female similar but with browner upperparts, yellow irides, and less uniform orange underparts. Juvenile has rufous-barred flanks and occasionally a mesial stripe, making them superficially similar to juvenile Grey-faced Buzzard, but that species has much longer and less pointed wings. Besra, Shikra, and Japanese Sparrowhawk have five fingers; Crested Goshawk and Eurasian Sparrowhawk have six.

claimText: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.

claimText: The Buteo buzzards present a stocky body and broad wings when in flight. Difficult to distinguish from Eastern Buzzard, but said to be darker brown overall, with dark carpal patch not contrasting with the rest of the wing as strongly. Can come in three distinct morphs: brown, rufous and dark. Brown morph with solid, brown wing lining and often possessing a pale breast 'belt' that separates the dark plumage of the belly from the strong upper breast streaking; tail also strongly barred. Rufous morph has dark brown underparts of brown morph replaced by warm rufous brown and less distinct tail barring. Dark morph has blackish-brown body plumage with pale flight feathers and a dark trailing edge to the wing. Crested Honey Buzzard shows a small protruding head and longer tail; Changeable Hawk-Eagle is larger with a prominent crest; Jerdon's Baza has a long crest and strongly barred underparts.
